``` > Every number in a playtest report describes the players who happened to turn > up. Bring in a different group and every number moves. This page is about how > far: what **sampling variability** is, how the **standard error** measures it, > and how a **confidence interval** turns one playtest's number into an honest > range for the population you care about. The playtest question running through > it: *"Build B sessions averaged 24 minutes. How sure can we be?"* ::: {.at-a-glance} **Time:** 15 minutes in class (the simulation figures); the rest is reading. **Before this:** [Distributions and Shape](05-distributions-and-shape.qmd), especially the normal distribution. **Key terms:** sampling variability, sampling distribution, standard error, central limit theorem, confidence interval, margin of error. **R introduced:** `sample()`, `replicate()`, `sqrt()`, `qt()`, `t.test()` for one group. ::: ## Learning Outcomes By the end of these notes you can: - explain why a second playtest with different players would give different numbers, even if nothing about the game changed; - describe a sampling distribution, and say what the standard error measures; - explain how sample size affects the standard error, and why quadrupling the players only halves it; - state the central limit theorem in plain English, and say why it matters for data that is not normal; - compute and interpret a 95% confidence interval for a mean, and say what the "95%" does and does not mean. --- ## Why This Matters for Playtesting [Planning a Playtest](01-planning-a-playtest.qmd#how-many-players) showed that a five-session playtest can report a frustration rate anywhere from 0% to 60% when the true rate is a third. That spread is not a flaw in the method. It is what happens whenever you measure some players and draw conclusions about all of them. **Every comparison in Part 4 rests on this page.** Build B's sessions were longer than Build A's. Is that because Build B is better, or because Build B happened to get the more patient players? You cannot answer that until you know how much a number would move by chance alone. That amount has a name, the standard error, and this page shows where it comes from. --- ## Sampling Variability Split the 120 *Tidebreak* sessions into four batches of 30, in the order they were recorded, and treat each as a separate playtest. Same game, same build mix, same procedure. The mean score of each batch: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} batch <- ceiling(seq_len(nrow(sessions)) / 30) round(tapply(sessions$score, batch, mean)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1 2 3 4 1550 1313 1462 1390 ``` ::: ::: Four playtests, four different answers, from 1313 to 1550. Nothing changed except which players were in each batch. **Sampling variability** is this: a different sample gives a different number, even from the same population. It is not a mistake and it cannot be avoided. The only question is how big it is, and that depends on two things: **how much the players differ** (the SD) and **how many of them you measured** (n). --- ## The Sampling Distribution To see sampling variability properly, you need many playtests, not four. Real studios cannot afford that, but a simulation can. Imagine the population of everyone who will ever play *Tidebreak*, and suppose their session lengths look exactly like the 120 you recorded. Build that population by copying the sessions a thousand times over, then run a thousand imaginary playtests of 30 players each, and record each playtest's mean: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pop <- rep(sessions$session_minutes, times = 1000) set.seed(7) means_30 <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(pop, 30))) ``` ::: `sample(pop, 30)` draws 30 players at random; `mean()` is that playtest's result; `replicate(1000, ...)` runs it a thousand times. The thousand means form the **sampling distribution**: the distribution of a summary across every playtest you might have run. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 3, 2, 1)) hist(pop, breaks = 26, col = pal$fill, border = "white", main = "Population", xlab = "Session length (minutes)", ylab = "", yaxt = "n", cex.main = 0.9) abline(v = pop_mean, col = pal$highlight, lwd = 2) hist(means_30, breaks = 30, freq = FALSE, col = pal$fill, border = "white", main = "1,000 playtest means, n = 30", xlim = range(pop), xlab = "Mean session length (minutes)", ylab = "", yaxt = "n", cex.main = 0.9) curve(dnorm(x, mean(means_30), sd(means_30)), add = TRUE, lwd = 2, col = pal$highlight) par(op) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Left: session length across the imaginary population, lopsided and two-humped. Right: the means of 1,000 playtests of 30 players drawn from it, which form a bell.](07-sample-to-population_files/figure-html/fig-sampling-dist-1.png){#fig-sampling-dist fig-alt='Two histograms. Left: the population of session lengths, piled up near 30 minutes with a second smaller hump around 12 minutes. Right: the distribution of 1,000 sample means, a narrow symmetric bell centred near 23 minutes, with a red normal curve laid over it that fits closely.' width=768} ::: ::: Two things stand out. **The means are centred on the truth.** The population mean is 22.8 minutes; the average of the thousand playtest means is 22.8. Any one playtest misses, but not systematically in one direction. **The means are far less spread out than the players.** Individual sessions run from 7.7 to 32 minutes. Playtest means of 30 players fall almost all between 19.9 and 25.3. Averaging cancels out most of the differences between players. --- ## The Standard Error The SD of the sampling distribution has its own name: the **standard error** (SE). It is the typical distance between one playtest's mean and the population's mean: **how far your number is likely to be off**. You never get to run a thousand playtests, but you do not need to. The standard error can be estimated from a single sample: $$\text{SE} = \frac{\text{SD}}{\sqrt{n}}$$ Check it against the simulation. The population SD is 7.73, so for n = 30 the formula gives 7.73 / √30 = 1.41. The SD of the thousand simulated means is 1.38. The formula works. **Bigger samples give smaller standard errors, but slowly.** Because n is under a square root, you need **four times** the players to **halve** the standard error: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} par(mar = c(4, 6, 1, 1)) stripchart(list("n = 10" = means_10, "n = 30" = means_30, "n = 100" = means_100), method = "jitter", jitter = 0.25, pch = 16, cex = 0.4, las = 1, col = adjustcolor(pal$line, alpha.f = 0.3), xlab = "Playtest mean session length (minutes)") abline(v = pop_mean, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = pal$highlight) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Means of 1,000 simulated playtests at three sizes. Each quadrupling of n roughly halves the spread.](07-sample-to-population_files/figure-html/fig-sample-size-se-1.png){#fig-sample-size-se fig-alt='Three horizontal strips of points. With n = 10 the playtest means spread widely around the dashed true mean; with n = 30 they are tighter; with n = 100 they cluster closely around it.' width=768} ::: ::: | Players per playtest | SE from the formula | SD of 1,000 simulated means | | :-: | :-: | :-: | | 10 | 2.44 | 2.45 | | 30 | 1.41 | 1.38 | | 100 | 0.77 | 0.79 | **SD and SE answer different questions.** The SD describes the players: how much one session differs from another. The SE describes your *estimate*: how much your mean would move if you ran the playtest again. More players does not make the players less varied, so the SD stays put; it makes your estimate steadier, so the SE shrinks. --- ## The Central Limit Theorem Look again at the left panel of @fig-sampling-dist. Session length is lopsided and two-humped, nothing like a bell. Yet the means on the right form a bell almost perfectly. That is the **central limit theorem**: **whatever shape the individual values have, the means of reasonably large samples are approximately normal.** The individual players can be skewed, bimodal or capped; their averages still pile up in a bell around the true mean. It is why the normal distribution from [Distributions and Shape](05-distributions-and-shape.qmd#the-normal-distribution) matters even for data that is not normal. The 68–95–99.7 rule does not describe the session lengths, but it does describe the sampling distribution of their mean. So about 95% of playtest means fall within 2 standard errors of the true mean. That single fact is what confidence intervals and t-tests are built on. **How large is "reasonably large"?** For mildly skewed data, 30 is usually plenty; the simulation above uses 30 and the bell is clear. For heavily skewed data, such as frame times with rare hitches, it takes more. --- ## Confidence Intervals If 95% of playtest means fall within about 2 SEs of the true mean, then turning it round, the true mean is within about 2 SEs of your playtest's mean 95% of the time. That range is a **95% confidence interval**: $$\text{mean} \pm \text{about } 2 \times \text{SE}$$ The "about 2" is 1.96 for large samples; for smaller ones R uses a slightly larger number from the **t distribution**, which allows for the SD itself being estimated from the sample. The part after the ± is the **margin of error**. **For real:** Build B's 60 sessions. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mins_b <- sessions$session_minutes[sessions$build == "B"] m <- mean(mins_b) se <- sd(mins_b) / sqrt(length(mins_b)) multiplier <- qt(0.975, df = length(mins_b) - 1) c(mean = m, se = se, multiplier = multiplier) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mean se multiplier 24.2416667 0.8962864 2.0009954 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} m + c(-1, 1) * multiplier * se ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 22.44820 26.03513 ``` ::: ::: And the same in one line, which is how you will usually do it: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} t.test(mins_b)$conf.int ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 22.44820 26.03513 attr(,"conf.level") [1] 0.95 ``` ::: ::: **In a report you would write:** "Build B sessions averaged 24.2 minutes (95% CI 22.4 to 26, n = 60)." The interval says the data is consistent with a population average anywhere from 22.4 to 26 minutes. That honesty is the point: a reader now knows how much weight the 24.2 can bear. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Going further: these sessions are not quite independent"} The interval treats Build B's 60 sessions as 60 independent observations. They are not: they come from 15 players who each played 4 times, and one player's sessions resemble each other. The honest effective sample size is somewhere between the number of players and the number of sessions, so the true interval is somewhat wider than this one. Handling repeated measurements properly needs methods beyond this module; the practical lesson is to report both counts ([rule 8](ten-rules.qmd)). ::: ### What "95%" means This is the most misread number in statistics. **The 95% describes the method, not this particular interval.** If you ran the playtest many times and computed an interval each time, about 95% of those intervals would contain the true population mean. Any one interval either contains it or does not; you never know which. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} miss <- cis[, 1] > pop_mean | cis[, 2] < pop_mean par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1)) plot(NA, xlim = range(cis), ylim = c(1, 20), yaxt = "n", xlab = "Mean session length (minutes)", ylab = "Playtest") axis(2, at = c(1, 5, 10, 15, 20), las = 1) segments(cis[, 1], 1:20, cis[, 2], 1:20, lwd = 2, col = ifelse(miss, pal$highlight, pal$line)) points(rowMeans(cis), 1:20, pch = 19, cex = 0.7, col = ifelse(miss, pal$highlight, pal$line)) abline(v = pop_mean, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = pal$guide) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Twenty simulated playtests of 30 players, each with its 95% confidence interval. The dashed line is the true population mean. Red intervals miss it.](07-sample-to-population_files/figure-html/fig-twenty-cis-1.png){#fig-twenty-cis fig-alt='Twenty horizontal line segments stacked vertically, each with a dot at its centre. A vertical dashed line marks the true mean. Most segments cross the dashed line; the ones that do not are drawn in red.' width=768} ::: ::: In this run, 1 of the 20 intervals missed the true mean, close to the one in twenty the method promises. A playtest that misses has done nothing wrong; it drew an unusual set of players, which is exactly what the 5% allows for. **So do not say** "there is a 95% chance the true mean is between 22.4 and 26". Say "the method that produced this interval captures the true mean 95% of the time", or, in a report, simply give the interval and let it stand for "the plausible range". **Wider means less certain.** An interval narrows with more players (a smaller SE) and widens with more varied players (a larger SD). A 99% interval is wider than a 95% one: more confidence costs precision. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Going further: the bootstrap"} The formula relies on the central limit theorem. The **bootstrap** gets an interval without it, by treating your sample as a stand-in for the population and resampling it. Draw 60 sessions *with replacement* from Build B's 60, take the mean, and repeat a thousand times; the middle 95% of those means is the interval. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(3) boot_means <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(mins_b, replace = TRUE))) quantile(boot_means, c(0.025, 0.975)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2.5% 97.5% 22.59825 25.83671 ``` ::: ::: It agrees closely with `t.test()`'s 22.4 to 26. The bootstrap earns its keep for summaries with no simple formula, such as a median or a 99th percentile: replace `mean` with `median` in the line above and it still works. ::: --- ## Worked Example **Build B sessions averaged 24 minutes. How sure can we be?** The draft report says: "Build B sessions last 24 minutes on average." **Step 1: what is the sample?** 60 sessions from 15 players, one playtest. A different group would give a different mean. **Step 2: how much would it move?** The SD of Build B's session lengths is 6.94 minutes. The standard error is that divided by √60: 0.9 minutes. A second playtest's mean would typically land within about 0.9 minutes of this one. **Step 3: give the range.** The 95% confidence interval is 22.4 to 26 minutes. **Step 4: rewrite.** "Build B sessions averaged 24.2 minutes (95% CI 22.4 to 26; 60 sessions from 15 players)." The claim is now as strong as the data, and no stronger. **Step 5: notice what is still missing.** This is one build on its own. Whether Build B's sessions are longer than Build A's is a different question, because both numbers wobble. Comparing two groups, and asking whether the gap could be chance, is [Comparing Groups](08-comparing-groups.qmd). --- ## Interpretation Guidance **What the data shows.** One playtest's mean: 24.2 minutes for Build B. **What the analysis suggests.** The population mean is plausibly anywhere from 22.4 to 26 minutes, with values near the centre of that range more plausible than values at its ends. **What can legitimately be concluded.** A range, not a point. A finding that depends on the exact value of a mean, such as "sessions must average 25 minutes", cannot be settled by a playtest whose interval spans both sides of 25. --- ## Common Mistakes **Treating one playtest's number as a fact about the game.** It is a fact about those players. Give the interval. **Confusing the SD and the SE.** The SD describes the players; the SE describes your estimate. Reporting an SE as if it were the spread of the players makes the players look far more alike than they are. **Reading "95%" as the chance this interval is right.** It describes how often the method works, not this interval. **Expecting a bigger sample to fix everything.** Four times the players halves the SE. Doubling the playtest buys less precision than it seems. **Forgetting that sessions are not players.** Repeated sessions from the same player are not independent, so an interval built on sessions is somewhat too narrow. Report both counts. **Assuming the central limit theorem rescues tiny samples.** With five players and skewed data, the sample mean is not reliably normal, and the interval is not reliable either. --- ## Practice Each takes two or three minutes. **1. Predict.** A playtest of 25 players gives an SE of 2 minutes. Roughly what SE would 100 players give? And 400? ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check your answer"} About 1 minute with 100 players (four times the players, half the SE) and about 0.5 with 400 (sixteen times the players, a quarter of the SE). Each halving costs four times as many players. ::: **2. Compute.** Find the 95% confidence interval for the mean session length of **Build A**, and compare its width with Build B's. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check your answer"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mins_a <- sessions$session_minutes[sessions$build == "A"] ci_a <- t.test(mins_a)$conf.int ci_a ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 19.15051 23.43949 attr(,"conf.level") [1] 0.95 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} diff(ci_a) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4.288983 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} diff(t.test(mins_b)$conf.int) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3.58693 ``` ::: ::: Build A's interval is 19.2 to 23.4 minutes, and it is wider: the same number of sessions, but Build A's session lengths are more spread out (SD 8.3 against 6.9), because of its two groups of players. ::: **3. Critique.** A report says: "Mean enjoyment was 4.1 (SE 0.08), so players agreed closely about how much they enjoyed it." What is wrong? ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check your answer"} The SE says how precisely the *mean* is known, not how much players agreed. With 120 sessions, the SE is small even if players disagreed widely. To describe agreement, report the SD or the distribution. (Enjoyment is also a 1 to 7 rating, so the distribution is the better summary anyway; see [Data, Variables and Types](03-data-and-types.qmd#the-rating-scale-question).) ::: **4. Interpret.** In @fig-twenty-cis, one of the red intervals came from a playtest. Did that playtest do anything wrong? ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check your answer"} No. It drew an unusual set of players by chance. A 95% method is designed to miss about one time in twenty, and nothing in the data warns you when it is your turn. That is why a single surprising result is a reason to run another playtest, not to redesign the game. ::: --- ## Summary - A different sample gives a different number. That is sampling variability, and it is unavoidable. - The sampling distribution is the distribution of a summary across every playtest you might have run. Its SD is the standard error: how far your estimate is typically off. - SE = SD / √n. Four times the players halves the SE. - The SD describes the players; the SE describes your estimate. - The central limit theorem: means of reasonably large samples are approximately normal, whatever the shape of the data. - A 95% confidence interval is about mean ± 2 SE. The 95% describes the method: it captures the true value in about 95% of playtests. - Report a mean with its interval and n. | Key term | Meaning | | :- | :- | | **Sampling variability** | Different samples from the same population give different results | | **Sampling distribution** | The distribution of a summary across many possible samples | | **Standard error** | The SD of the sampling distribution: how far an estimate is typically off | | **Central limit theorem** | Means of reasonably large samples are approximately normal | | **Confidence interval** | A range of plausible values for the population, given the sample | | **Margin of error** | The part after the ± in a confidence interval | | **Bootstrap** | Estimating a sampling distribution by resampling your own sample | --- ## Links - [Ten Rules](ten-rules.qmd): rule 8 (small samples lie confidently) - [Statistics Reference: from sample to population](../reference/reference-statistics.qmd#from-sample-to-population) - [Lab 02: Comparing Builds](../labs/comparing-builds.qmd), Part B - [Week 2 demo](../demos/week-2.qmd) - Next: [Comparing Groups](08-comparing-groups.qmd) --- ## Reflective Questions - Your playtest found a mean session length of 24 minutes, and your producer wants "the number". Do you give them 24, or the interval? What do you say to justify your choice? - Doubling the playtest from 30 to 60 players narrows the interval by less than a third. When is that worth the cost, and when is it not? - The central limit theorem rescues means from skewed data. Does it rescue the 99th percentile of frame time? What would you do instead? - Your interval for Build B is built on sessions, but players played four sessions each. Is the true interval wider or narrower, and why does it matter for a design decision?
